title: Returning to Key Stage 3: Design Assessment That Reflects the Curriculum
author: Sarah Findlater
summary: In the fifth installment of her Key Stage 3 curriculum series, Sarah Findlater argues that assessment often enters planning too late and that a well-written, consistently marked task can still yield poor evidence if it does not match what the curriculum has actually taught. She works through design choices: begin with the purpose and the decision the evidence will inform, assess only learning students have experienced, create enough distance from taught material to see independence without springing surprises, and look across the whole assessment sequence for gaps. She also asks teachers to check what else a task demands, to let criteria follow the curriculum rather than inherited rubrics, and to treat a common task as one piece of evidence alongside professional judgement and moderation. She closes with five tests, purpose, curriculum, validity, coverage and response, for reviewing any assessment.
points: Start with the decision an assessment will inform, because a task designed for one purpose, such as retrieval or reporting, rarely serves another.
A task is only valid evidence if its demands trace back to what students were actually taught and practised, so a broad essay can wrongly signal that students cannot interpret character.
The right distance between practice and the assessment lets students make some decisions independently without mistaking rehearsal for independence or novelty for failure.
Assessment sequences shape curriculum, since whatever recurs in the schedule gets the teaching time, so a narrow sequence narrows what students experience.
Results should stay connected to the work behind them, because two students with the same mark may need very different next steps.
quotes: A credible-looking assessment could produce poor evidence if it required knowledge, independence or a form of response that the curriculum had not yet developed.
Consistent marking can make a task more dependable, but it cannot make the wrong task reveal the intended learning.
If students repeatedly answer the assessment question, memorise an interpretation prepared in class or follow a structure designed for that specific response, their completed work may appear secure.
Asking whether a task looked sufficiently demanding was less useful than asking which part of progression it would make visible.
What appears repeatedly in an assessment schedule receives time and attention in teaching. Students notice what counts.
Adding incidental difficulty does not make an assessment more rigorous.
Descriptors that move from “some” evidence to “a range” and then a “wide range” can tell a teacher surprisingly little about how a student’s thinking has developed.
Two students with the same mark may need different teaching. One may understand the text but struggle to organise a response; another may write fluently while making an imprecise interpretation.
